items.question_text: A 58-year-old woman attends a Melbourne general practice on a Thursday afternoon for a repeat of transdermal oestradiol, which she has used since a surgical menopause at 49. She works as a school registrar, walks to the station each day, and has no chest pain, breast lump, nipple discharge, skin dimpling, or axillary swelling. Her mother is alive at 84 and has never had cancer. An aunt had breast cancer at 71 and is also alive. She took the oral contraceptive pill for less than a year in her twenties, had two children before 30, and breastfed both. She drinks a glass of wine on weekends and has never smoked. Her last BreastScreen report, 26 months ago, was normal and described heterogeneously dense tissue. She has spent the week reading online forums in which women with dense breasts were told that mammography is almost useless and that they should pay for a private contrast MRI every year. A private radiologist who imaged her shoulder last year made a similar offhand comment about density. Her BMI is 27. Examination of both breasts and axillae is normal. There is no skin change and no nipple retraction. She takes no other medicines and has no implants. A recent full blood count, done for fatigue that resolved, was normal. She is not on an anticoagulant. Her blood pressure today is 128/76. She is not diabetic. A cholesterol check last month was acceptable. She can attend a screening centre within two weeks. Her GP notes that she is squarely inside the invited age band and that her family history does not meet criteria for a familial cancer clinic. She has capacity, is not pregnant, and asks, plainly, what she should actually do this year. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Book the next BreastScreen mammogram now
Arrange annual breast MRI as her population screening test
Replace mammography with screening ultrasound because the last report mentioned density
Measure CA 15-3 today and screen only if it is raised
Defer all imaging until 65 because the last mammogram was normal
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Book the next BreastScreen mammogram now

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A 58-year-old woman attends a Melbourne general practice on a Thursday afternoon for a repeat of transdermal oestradiol, which she has used since a surgical menopause at 49. She works as a school registrar, walks to the station each day, and has no chest pain, breast lump, nipple discharge, skin dimpling, or axillary swelling. Her mother is alive at 84 and has never had cancer.

2. THE RULE
Symptom-free women aged 50-74 are invited to BreastScreen every 2 years; women 40-49 and 75+ may self-refer, and asymptomatic men are not screened.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
She is symptom-free, 58, and 26 months past a normal mammogram, so she is due for the BreastScreen test. Heterogeneous density and an aunt diagnosed at 71 do not move her onto MRI. Hormone therapy is not a reason to change the program test.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Arrange annual breast MRI as her population screening test: MRI is used in selected high-risk pathways. An aunt at 71 and a density comment do not establish that pathway.
C. Replace mammography with screening ultrasound because the last report mentioned density: Ultrasound is not the BreastScreen test, and density alone does not retire mammography.
D. Measure CA 15-3 today and screen only if it is raised: A tumour marker is not a screening test and would not clear her for a longer interval.
E. Defer all imaging until 65 because the last mammogram was normal: A normal result restarts the 2-year interval. It does not grant a 7-year gap.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Symptom-free women aged 50-74 are invited to BreastScreen every 2 years; women 40-49 and 75+ may self-refer, and asymptomatic men are not screened.

items.question_text: A 46-year-old woman in Adelaide has asked the receptionist for a BreastScreen referral after a friend said free mammograms do not start until 50 and that asking earlier is a waste of everyone's time. She has no lump, pain, nipple change, or skin thickening. Her sister had a fibroadenoma excised at 29. There is no relative with breast or ovarian cancer. She is otherwise well, has never had breast imaging, had one child at 32, and breastfed for four months. She works in a call centre, does not smoke, and drinks rarely. She is anxious because a colleague was diagnosed at 48, and she has convinced herself that waiting until 50 is reckless. On examination both breasts are normal, with no axillary nodes. She is not pregnant. She asks whether booking now is pointless, whether she will be turned away, and whether she should instead pay for a private ultrasound to be safe. A local radiology group has already quoted her $480 for a bilateral ultrasound and mammogram. Her GP records show no breast complaint in six years at the practice. There is no chest-wall radiation in her history. A cousin had a benign cyst drained at 40. She has private health insurance and wants a clear answer on whether the public system will accept her at 46. Blood pressure is 122/74. She takes no regular medicines. A recent cervical screen was normal. She can attend a centre next week if advised. Examination today adds nothing. What is the most appropriate advice about BreastScreen?
options: Tell her she is ineligible for a free mammogram until she turns 50
A normal examination today replaces imaging until 50
Screen with ultrasound every year until she enters the invitation group
She can book a BreastScreen mammogram now, but she will not be routinely invited until 50
Start annual mammography from today until 74 because she has asked early
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. She can book a BreastScreen mammogram now, but she will not be routinely invited until 50

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
At 46 she can book BreastScreen but is not in the routine invitation group, and a fibroadenoma in a sister does not create an annual pathway.

2. THE RULE
Symptom-free women aged 50-74 are invited to BreastScreen every 2 years; women 40-49 and 75+ may self-refer, and asymptomatic men are not screened.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Invitation and access are different. BreastScreen invites women aged 50–74. From 40 she may still book a free mammogram every 2 years. A sister's fibroadenoma is not a familial-cancer indication, so she does not need annual imaging.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Tell her she is ineligible for a free mammogram until she turns 50: That confuses the invitation letter with the age from which she can attend.
B. A normal examination today replaces imaging until 50: Examination does not answer the screening question she asked.
C. Screen with ultrasound every year until she enters the invitation group: Ultrasound is not the population test at 46.
E. Start annual mammography from today until 74 because she has asked early: Asking early does not shorten the interval from 2 years.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Invitation age is 50–74. Attendance is open from 40.

items.question_text: A 61-year-old woman in Brisbane notices a new hard lump in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast while showering. It has been there for three weeks. She had a normal BreastScreen mammogram 14 months ago. There is no nipple discharge. She is a non-smoker, takes perindopril for hypertension, and has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. On examination there is a 2 cm firm, irregular mass, tethered to skin, with a palpable left axillary node. She is frightened and asks whether she should simply wait for her next BreastScreen invitation, which she believes is the proper pathway, or book the routine screening mammogram a few months early. Her sister has told her that screening clinics are faster than hospital clinics. She has no fever, no recent trauma, and no signs of infection. The remainder of the examination is normal. She is systemically well, weight stable, and has no bone pain. A BreastScreen letter from 14 months ago is in her bag and is normal. The axillary node is firm and about 1.5 cm. She is post-menopausal on no hormone therapy. Her sister has offered to drive her to a BreastScreen van in the suburb next week. The GP can feel the mass and the node. Bloods last month were unremarkable. She is not anticoagulated. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Request CA 15-3 and a chest X-ray as the first screen
Reassure her that a mobile lump under 45 can be reviewed in 6 months
Start tamoxifen now and image only if the lump is still there in 3 months
Use the BreastScreen appointment and review her once the screening report returns
Refer for diagnostic triple assessment rather than a screening mammogram
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Refer for diagnostic triple assessment rather than a screening mammogram

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A 3-week hard breast lump needs diagnostic triple assessment. A convenient BreastScreen slot does not convert it into a screening episode.

2. THE RULE
A breast symptom or high familial risk needs diagnostic or specialist assessment, not a routine BreastScreen mammogram.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
A new hard lump is a symptom. BreastScreen is for women without breast symptoms, and a screening slot does not investigate a palpable mass. She needs diagnostic triple assessment: clinical review, diagnostic imaging, and needle biopsy as indicated.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Request CA 15-3 and a chest X-ray as the first screen: Neither assesses a palpable breast mass.
B. Reassure her that a mobile lump under 45 can be reviewed in 6 months: Mobility and age do not make a new hard lump safe to watch.
C. Start tamoxifen now and image only if the lump is still there in 3 months: Endocrine therapy is not a test and not a holding measure.
D. Use the BreastScreen appointment and review her once the screening report returns: The free slot is the trap. A screening program should not be used to work up a lump, and 10 days on that list is the wrong queue.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Symptoms leave BreastScreen.

---

items.question_text: A 77-year-old woman in Hobart has not been invited to BreastScreen for two years. She is well, has no breast symptom, and had normal screens throughout her sixties. Her daughter has read that screening stops at 74 and has told her she is no longer allowed to attend. She is a retired teacher, lives alone, drives, and has no cognitive impairment. There is no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. She takes a statin and vitamin D. Examination is normal. She asks whether the program has closed to her permanently, whether attending would be against the rules, and whether she should instead pay for a private mammogram every year for the rest of her life. She has attended BreastScreen regularly since 52 and has every normal report in a folder at home. Her daughter read a news article saying the program ends at 74 and has booked her a private annual mammogram at $320 a time. She is a retired teacher, lives alone, drives, and manages her own medicines. There is no cognitive impairment. She takes atorvastatin and vitamin D only. There is no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Examination today is normal, with no mass and no node. She is not frail. Her GP estimates her life expectancy is well beyond five years. She asks whether the program has closed to her permanently, whether attending would be against the rules, and whether private imaging every year is now her only option. The question is invitation versus access after 74. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Transfer her to annual screening MRI because invitation has stopped
Replace mammography with 2-yearly clinical examination only
She is no longer invited, but she may choose to book BreastScreen after a discussion of benefit
She must continue annual mammography until 80 to stay enrolled
Further mammography is contraindicated once she is over 74
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. She is no longer invited, but she may choose to book BreastScreen after a discussion of benefit

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
After 74 she is no longer invited, but mammography is not forbidden. She can still choose BreastScreen.

2. THE RULE
Symptom-free women aged 50-74 are invited to BreastScreen every 2 years; women 40-49 and 75+ may self-refer, and asymptomatic men are not screened.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Active invitation stops after 74. That is not a ban. A well 76-year-old with no breast symptoms may choose to keep attending after a discussion of benefit, overdiagnosis, and competing health problems. Her last screen was 18 months ago, so she is not even due today.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Transfer her to annual screening MRI because invitation has stopped: Loss of a reminder does not create an MRI pathway.
B. Replace mammography with 2-yearly clinical examination only: Examination is not the screening test she has been having.
D. She must continue annual mammography until 80 to stay enrolled: There is no compulsory annual program to 80.
E. Further mammography is contraindicated once she is over 74: The friend has turned the end of invitation into a prohibition.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
End of invitation is not a contraindication.

---

items.question_text: A 42-year-old woman is found to carry a pathogenic BRCA1 variant after her sister died of ovarian cancer at 46. She has no breast symptom. She has been told by a relative to just join BreastScreen early and have an ordinary mammogram every two years like everyone else. She has two children, breastfed both, does not smoke, and has not had risk-reducing surgery. Examination of breasts and axillae is normal. She is not pregnant. There is no lump. Her GP has the genetic report. A colleague suggests that because she is under 50 she cannot access any imaging at all, and another suggests a single private ultrasound and discharge. The BRCA1 result arrived last week from a familial cancer service that tested her after her sister's death. She has no breast symptom, no ovarian symptom, and has not had risk-reducing surgery. She has two children, breastfed both, and does not smoke. A relative has told her to join BreastScreen early and have an ordinary mammogram every two years. She has been reading conflicting advice online, some of it about MRI and some about ultrasound. Examination of breasts and axillae is normal. She is not pregnant. There is no lump. Her GP has the genetic report in the file. A colleague has suggested she is too young for any imaging, and another has suggested a single private ultrasound and discharge. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Bilateral mastectomy must be booked before any further imaging or pregnancy care
Routine BreastScreen from age 50 is sufficient for a BRCA1 carrier
Population ultrasound from age 30 can replace specialist review during pregnancy
Defer every breast decision until she has finished childbearing
Refer to a familial cancer service for an intensified surveillance plan
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Refer to a familial cancer service for an intensified surveillance plan

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
BRCA1 is not covered by waiting for BreastScreen at 50. She should be referred to a familial cancer service, not booked for immediate mastectomy.

2. THE RULE
A breast symptom or high familial risk needs diagnostic or specialist assessment, not a routine BreastScreen mammogram.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
A pathogenic BRCA1 variant is not average risk, and pregnancy does not park that fact until BreastScreen invitation at 50. She needs a familial cancer service to plan surveillance, usually earlier and with MRI considered. Surgery may be discussed later. It is not an emergency order before antenatal care.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Bilateral mastectomy must be booked before any further imaging or pregnancy care: Risk-reducing surgery is a counselled option, not the mandatory next booking.
B. Routine BreastScreen from age 50 is sufficient for a BRCA1 carrier: That leaflet is the average-risk rule. The mutation is the fact that kills it.
C. Population ultrasound from age 30 can replace specialist review during pregnancy: Ultrasound is not a population substitute for high-risk care.
D. Defer every breast decision until she has finished childbearing: Family completion is not the surveillance clock.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Population invitation ages assume average risk.

---

items.question_text: A 55-year-old man asks whether he should enrol in BreastScreen because his mother had breast cancer at 78. He has no breast lump, nipple discharge, or skin change. He is well, takes no medicines, and has never had breast imaging. There is no other family history. He works as a driver and is a non-smoker. Examination shows no mass and no axillary node. He has read that men can get breast cancer and assumes there must be a population mammography program for asymptomatic men, parallel to the women's program. He asks for the invitation letter and the two-yearly recall. His GP notes he is asymptomatic and has no personal high-risk feature. He is 55, well, and takes no medicines. His mother had breast cancer at 78 and is alive. He has no breast lump, no nipple discharge, and no skin change. There is no other family history of breast or ovarian cancer. He works as a driver and has never smoked. Examination shows no mass and no axillary node. He has read that men can get breast cancer and assumes there is a population mammography program for asymptomatic men, with invitation letters and two-yearly recall, parallel to the women's program. He has asked the receptionist for the enrolment form. He is asymptomatic and has no personal high-risk feature such as prior chest radiation or a known pathogenic variant. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Start tamoxifen for 5 years as the male prevention program
Annual screening ultrasound until 74 is the male equivalent
Check CA 15-3 every 2 years alongside his lipid tests
Population breast screening is not offered to an asymptomatic man
Enrol him for 2-yearly mammography if he is willing to pay
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Population breast screening is not offered to an asymptomatic man

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
An asymptomatic man is not enrolled in BreastScreen, including if he offers to pay.

2. THE RULE
Symptom-free women aged 50-74 are invited to BreastScreen every 2 years; women 40-49 and 75+ may self-refer, and asymptomatic men are not screened.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
BreastScreen is a population program for women. Willingness to pay does not create a male invitation cohort. He has no lump, so this is not a diagnostic referral either.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Start tamoxifen for 5 years as the male prevention program: Chemoprevention is not indicated by a request for enrolment.
B. Annual screening ultrasound until 74 is the male equivalent: There is no male ultrasound program shadowing BreastScreen.
C. Check CA 15-3 every 2 years alongside his lipid tests: A marker is not screening.
E. Enrol him for 2-yearly mammography if he is willing to pay: Payment does not turn a women's screening program into a male one.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
BreastScreen does not have a male population arm.

---

items.question_text: A 47-year-old man in Perth asks for a bowel cancer screening kit. A friend told him the government posts them from 40. He has no rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, weight loss, or anaemia. His father had a polyp removed at 72. He is otherwise well, BMI 29, non-smoker. He has never had a colonoscopy. He is keen to get on the list and is irritated that nothing has arrived in the post. Examination is unremarkable and there is no abdominal mass. He is 47, BMI 29, and a non-smoker. He has no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit, no weight loss, and no anaemia on a blood count done last month for an insurance medical. His father had a polyp removed at 72. He has never had a colonoscopy. A friend told him kits are posted from age 40, and he is irritated that nothing has arrived. Examination shows no abdominal mass. He asks whether he can request a free kit now or must wait for the automatic mail-out at 50. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: The kit is only for people who have already noticed bleeding
He can request a free kit now, and automatic mailing starts at 50
Book colonoscopy as the first program test because his wife was invited
He is ineligible until his 50th birthday, so do not request a kit
A kit should already have been mailed automatically at 45
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. He can request a free kit now, and automatic mailing starts at 50

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
At 47 he requests a bowel kit. The mailed kit his wife received is the 50–74 path, not proof he was missed.

2. THE RULE
People aged 45-49 may request a free NBCSP iFOBT kit, automatic mail-out runs from 50 to 74, and recent colonoscopy surveillance replaces the kit.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
Since 1 July 2024 the program age is 45–74. At 47 he requests the first kit. His wife's mailed kit reflects the 50–74 path, not a missed invitation. He has no symptoms, so colonoscopy is not the entry test.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. The kit is only for people who have already noticed bleeding: Bleeding would take him off the screening kit.
C. Book colonoscopy as the first program test because his wife was invited: Her invitation does not promote him to colonoscopy.
D. He is ineligible until his 50th birthday, so do not request a kit: That is the pre-2024 start age. Eligibility and automatic mail are no longer the same birthday.
E. A kit should already have been mailed automatically at 45: The first kit at 45–49 is requested.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
45–49 request the first kit. 50–74 are mailed one.

---

items.question_text: A 62-year-old woman receives her National Bowel Cancer Screening kit in the mail. She has no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit, and no weight loss. She had a normal colonoscopy eight years ago for a positive kit at the time. She asks if she can ignore the mail-out. There is no family history of colorectal cancer. Examination is normal. She is 62 and has just received her National Bowel Cancer Screening kit. She has no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit, and no weight loss. She had a normal colonoscopy eight years ago after a previous positive kit. She takes a statin and is otherwise well. There is no family history of colorectal cancer. She believes the old colonoscopy covers her for life and asks if she can ignore the mail-out. Examination is normal. Haemoglobin last year was normal. The question is whether she completes this kit. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Complete and return the kit
Cancel it and request a CEA with her annual lipids
Keep the kit until she next sees blood, then post it
Discard the kit and book a screening colonoscopy because she is over 60
Do the kit only if a fresh full blood count shows anaemia
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Complete and return the kit

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
An asymptomatic 63-year-old who receives a kit should complete it. A friend's colonoscopy and old haemorrhoids do not replace the kit.

2. THE RULE
People aged 45-49 may request a free NBCSP iFOBT kit, automatic mail-out runs from 50 to 74, and recent colonoscopy surveillance replaces the kit.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
She is in the mailed cohort and has no current bowel symptoms. Old treated haemorrhoids do not upgrade her to primary colonoscopy. The program test is the immunochemical kit.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Cancel it and request a CEA with her annual lipids: CEA is not the population test.
C. Keep the kit until she next sees blood, then post it: The kit is for people without bleeding. Waiting for a symptom misses the point.
D. Discard the kit and book a screening colonoscopy because she is over 60: Age over 60 is why she was mailed a kit, not a reason to skip it for colonoscopy.

She asks if she can wait for the five-year recall because the last test was normal. Examination today shows a contact bleed from the cervix. There is no uterine mass on abdominal palpation and no adnexal tenderness. She is not pregnant. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Arrange a self-collected sample in 12 months and do nothing before then
Take a routine screening test and review in 5 years if HPV is not detected
Give a further HPV vaccine dose today as the investigation
Reassure her that bleeding under 30 in a vaccinated woman needs no test
Assess the bleeding as a symptom, including a diagnostic co-test, rather than a routine screen
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Assess the bleeding as a symptom, including a diagnostic co-test, rather than a routine screen

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Six weeks of postcoital bleeding needs diagnostic assessment and a co-test. A routine 5-year screening plan does not clear it.

2. THE RULE
HPV 16/18 is referred for colposcopy regardless of cytology, other oncogenic HPV is retested in 12 months, and abnormal bleeding is investigated as a symptom, not screened.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
Postcoital bleeding is a symptom. A plan to wait 5 years if HPV is absent does not investigate it. She needs clinical assessment and a diagnostic HPV plus liquid-based cytology co-test, with referral if the cervix cannot be seen or looks abnormal. Vaccination does not explain 6 weeks of bleeding, and self-collection does not provide cytology.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Arrange a self-collected sample in 12 months and do nothing before then: That borrows the intermediate-risk interval and skips cytology.
B. Take a routine screening test and review in 5 years if HPV is not detected: A negative screen would be a false ending for a symptom.
C. Give a further HPV vaccine dose today as the investigation: Vaccine is prevention, not a test for bleeding.
D. Reassure her that bleeding under 30 in a vaccinated woman needs no test: Age and vaccine status do not retire postcoital bleeding.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Symptoms are not managed on the screening interval.

---

items.question_text: A 33-year-old woman is eligible for cervical screening and is not overdue. She has declined a speculum examination before because of discomfort, and she asks about self-collection. A friend has told her that self-collection is only offered to women who have already missed their test, as a catch-up measure for the overdue. She is asymptomatic. There is no postcoital bleeding. She would prefer to avoid a speculum if the option is open to her. She does not have to be overdue first. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Self-collection is available only because she would otherwise be overdue
She may choose a self-collected HPV sample as an eligible participant
Offer colposcopy as the alternative to a speculum examination
Declining a speculum ends her screening until she accepts one
She must have a conventional Pap smear instead of an HPV test
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. She may choose a self-collected HPV sample as an eligible participant

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
An eligible woman who declines a speculum may self-collect. She does not need to be overdue.

2. THE RULE
Routine HPV-based cervical screening runs from 25 to 74 every 5 years after a negative test, with self-collection an option for any eligible participant.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
Since 1 July 2022, anyone eligible may choose self-collection. It is not restricted to people who are overdue. She is due and asymptomatic, so a self-collected HPV sample is an acceptable program test. If it finds non-16/18 HPV she will still need a practitioner sample for cytology.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Self-collection is available only because she would otherwise be overdue: The poster is the old rule, from before July 2022.
C. Offer colposcopy as the alternative to a speculum examination: Colposcopy is a higher-risk referral, not the offer for a due screen.
D. Declining a speculum ends her screening until she accepts one: The program now has another collection method.
E. She must have a conventional Pap smear instead of an HPV test: Cytology alone is not the primary test.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Universal self-collection choice dates from 1 July 2022.

---

items.question_text: A 48-year-old woman asks when her next Cervical Screening Test is due. Three years ago she had a hysterectomy for fibroids. Histology was benign, with no CIN and no malignancy. She has never had an abnormal smear or a previous positive HPV test. She is asymptomatic. She assumes the screening schedule continues after the operation in the same way it would if the cervix were still present. She does not have a next due date on the program. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Colposcopy, because a reminder after hysterectomy implies higher risk
Vault cytology every 5 years until 74, because the register has written
She can leave routine cervical screening
HPV vaccination now, followed by vault smears
Self-collection every 2 years is the correct vault program
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. She can leave routine cervical screening

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Total hysterectomy for fibroids, cervix removed, no CIN and no bleeding, ends routine cervical screening despite the reminder.

2. THE RULE
Routine HPV-based cervical screening runs from 25 to 74 every 5 years after a negative test, with self-collection an option for any eligible participant.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Routine screening is for people with a cervix. Hers was removed for fibroids, with no CIN and no bleeding, so she does not continue vault screening to please the register. Vault tests still matter after hysterectomy for high-grade CIN or cancer, which this note is not.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Colposcopy, because a reminder after hysterectomy implies higher risk: A letter is not a higher-risk result.
B. Vault cytology every 5 years until 74, because the register has written: The letter is the trap. A reminder does not recreate an indication.
D. HPV vaccination now, followed by vault smears: Vaccination does not set a vault-smear program.
E. Self-collection every 2 years is the correct vault program: Self-collection is not a 2-year vault scheme.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
No cervix and no high-grade history means exit from routine screening.

---

items.question_text: A 62-year-old man asks about lung cancer screening. He has smoked 20 cigarettes a day since he was 18 and still smokes. There is no cough, no haemoptysis, no chest pain, and no weight loss. A chest X-ray done for a visa two years ago was reported normal, and he assumes that a chest X-ray is the screening test, because that is what his father had. Pack-years are well above the program threshold. He has no symptom that would move him from screening into a diagnostic pathway. He is otherwise well and can attend a program site. What is the most appropriate screening test if he is eligible?
options: Collect yearly sputum cytology as the program entry test
Delay any request until he has quit for 4 weeks
Arrange an annual chest X-ray, as his brother had
Tell him screening does not start until he turns 65
Offer low-dose CT through the National Lung Cancer Screening Program
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Offer low-dose CT through the National Lung Cancer Screening Program

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
An asymptomatic 61-year-old with about 40 pack-years who still smokes is offered low-dose CT, not a chest X-ray, and he need not quit first.

2. THE RULE
Lung cancer screening is 2-yearly low-dose CT for asymptomatic people aged 50-70 with at least 30 pack-years who smoke or quit within 10 years; symptoms need investigation.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
He is 61, asymptomatic for cancer, currently smoking, and has about 40 pack-years. That meets the National Lung Cancer Screening Program, which uses low-dose CT and started on 1 July 2025. A smoker's cough without haemoptysis or weight loss does not block entry. Quitting is offered. It is not a precondition.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Collect yearly sputum cytology as the program entry test: Sputum cytology is not the program.
B. Delay any request until he has quit for 4 weeks: He does not have to quit before a request can be made.
C. Arrange an annual chest X-ray, as his brother had: The brother's program is the retired test.
D. Tell him screening does not start until he turns 65: The age band is 50–70.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Entry is age 50–70, at least 30 pack-years, current smoking or quit within 10 years.

---

items.question_text: A 64-year-old woman asks to enter the national lung cancer screening program. She smoked 25 cigarettes a day from the age of 20 to 50, then quit. She has not smoked for 14 years. There is no cough, no haemoptysis, no chest pain, and no weight loss. She has seen advertising for the program and believes her heavy past smoking makes her eligible. Eligibility for former smokers requires that they quit within the last 10 years. Fourteen years is outside that window. What is the most appropriate advice about eligibility to enter?
options: Enroll her on pack-years alone and ignore the quit date
She is not eligible to enter the program
Offer annual chest X-ray for 5 years because she is outside the CT rule
Use sputum cytology as the substitute entry test
Sign the program request for a low-dose CT
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. She is not eligible to enter the program

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A first lung-screening request is not eligible if she quit 12 years ago, even with 35 pack-years.

2. THE RULE
Lung cancer screening is 2-yearly low-dose CT for asymptomatic people aged 50-70 with at least 30 pack-years who smoke or quit within 10 years; symptoms need investigation.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
New entry needs age 50–70, at least 30 pack-years, no suggestive symptoms, and current smoking or quit within 10 years. She quit 12 years ago and has never been enrolled. People already in the program may continue after they pass 10 years quit. That continuation rule does not open the door for a first request.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Enroll her on pack-years alone and ignore the quit date: Pack-years are necessary and not sufficient.
C. Offer annual chest X-ray for 5 years because she is outside the CT rule: Chest X-ray is not the fallback program.
D. Use sputum cytology as the substitute entry test: There is no sputum pathway for people outside the CT rule.
E. Sign the program request for a low-dose CT: The pack-years are enough. The quit interval is the fact that blocks entry.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
The entry quit-window is 10 years.

---

items.question_text: A 59-year-old man who still smokes, with a 40 pack-year history, attends after coughing up about a tablespoon of blood on two mornings this week. He has no fever and no chest pain. He has seen the lung screening advertisements and asks for a low-dose CT like the ads, rather than a diagnostic clinic appointment. He has no previous chest imaging. Enrolment in the screening program is the wrong pathway for someone who is bleeding. He needs assessment of the haemoptysis. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Send sputum cytology as the program entry test
Arrange a chest X-ray in 6 months and then decide about screening
Ask him to quit for 4 weeks and then sign the screening form
Investigate the haemoptysis rather than enrol him in screening
Complete the screening request for a low-dose CT
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Investigate the haemoptysis rather than enrol him in screening

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Haemoptysis takes him out of the lung screening program and into diagnostic assessment, even though his pack-years would otherwise qualify.

2. THE RULE
Lung cancer screening is 2-yearly low-dose CT for asymptomatic people aged 50-70 with at least 30 pack-years who smoke or quit within 10 years; symptoms need investigation.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Haemoptysis is a symptom suggestive of lung cancer. The program is for people without those symptoms. A free low-dose CT form is the wrong request. He needs diagnostic assessment. Quitting does not come before that.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Send sputum cytology as the program entry test: Sputum cytology is not the entry test.
B. Arrange a chest X-ray in 6 months and then decide about screening: Delay and a screening X-ray both miss the symptom.
C. Ask him to quit for 4 weeks and then sign the screening form: Cessation is not the investigation, and it would not restore screening eligibility while he is bleeding.
E. Complete the screening request for a low-dose CT: He meets the smoking numbers. The blood is the fact that takes him off the form.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
The program requires no symptoms suggestive of lung cancer.

items.question_text: A 55-year-old man asks for lung cancer screening because he is over 50 and once smoked. He smoked socially, a few cigarettes at weekends, for about five years in his twenties, and quit at 30. He is asymptomatic, with no cough, no haemoptysis, and no weight loss. options: She can self-request a screening PET scan
She must wait until 55 even if the pack-years later qualify
She is eligible on age and current smoking
She does not meet the pack-year threshold to enter
Offer annual chest X-ray because she is under 30 pack-years
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. She does not meet the pack-year threshold to enter

---

Ten cigarettes a day for 20 years is 10 pack-years, below the 30 required to enter lung screening.

2. THE RULE
Lung cancer screening is 2-yearly low-dose CT for asymptomatic people aged 50-70 with at least 30 pack-years who smoke or quit within 10 years; symptoms need investigation.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Ten cigarettes a day for 20 years is 10 pack-years. Entry needs at least 30, plus age 50–70 and current smoking or quit within 10 years, without symptoms. The poster omitted the pack-year line. A chest X-ray or PET is not the alternative program.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. She can self-request a screening PET scan: PET is not the screening test.
B. She must wait until 55 even if the pack-years later qualify: The age floor is 50.
C. She is eligible on age and current smoking: Those are two of the rules. Pack-years are the third, and she fails it.
E. Offer annual chest X-ray because she is under 30 pack-years: Being under the threshold does not create an X-ray program.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Pack-years are packs per day times years.

items.question_text: A 54-year-old man with no urinary symptoms attends asking to join the national PSA screening program. He has read about BreastScreen and the bowel kit program and assumes there is an equivalent national program for prostate cancer, with invitation letters and a fixed recall interval. There is no family history of prostate cancer. Examination is normal. He is not on a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor. He is asymptomatic. Opportunistic discussion of the PSA test is a different conversation from enrolment in a program. The answer to the question he has asked is that no such program exists. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: He will be mailed a PSA kit every 2 years, like the bowel program
Annual PSA is required for men from 50 to 74
There is no national PSA screening program to enrol him in
A normal PSA today would end any later discussion of prostate tests
A prostate MRI every 2 years is the population screening test
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. There is no national PSA screening program to enrol him in

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
There is no national PSA program to enrol him in. A request can lead to a shared decision, not a mail-out.

2. THE RULE
Australia has no national population screening program for prostate (PSA), skin or ovarian cancer; only breast, bowel, cervical and lung programs exist.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Australia does not run a population PSA program and does not mail PSA kits. A man who asks can have a shared discussion of benefit and harm. That discussion is not enrolment, and MRI is not a population screen.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. He will be mailed a PSA kit every 2 years, like the bowel program: He is mapping the bowel register onto a program that does not exist.
B. Annual PSA is required for men from 50 to 74: There is no required annual cohort.
D. A normal PSA today would end any later discussion of prostate tests: One result is not an exit rule from a program that is not running.
E. A prostate MRI every 2 years is the population screening test: MRI is not a population program.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Do not describe PSA as a mailed national program.

items.question_text: A 51-year-old woman at average risk asks for a yearly CA 125 blood test and a pelvic ultrasound to screen for ovarian cancer. She has no pelvic pain, no bloating, no urinary change, and no postmenopausal bleeding. There is no significant family history of ovarian, breast, or related cancers. A friend has these tests yearly and has told her this is standard screening, like a mammogram. Ordering them every year would be an unproven add-on, not screening. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: A single normal CA 125 today ends her familial risk
Population ovarian screening is not recommended on this history
CA 125 every 6 months can replace the ultrasound
Enrol her in annual CA 125 and pelvic ultrasound
Start a combined oral contraceptive as the screening test
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Population ovarian screening is not recommended on this history

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Annual CA 125 and ultrasound are not a screening program for an asymptomatic woman whose only affected relative was diagnosed at 72.

2. THE RULE
Australia has no national population screening program for prostate (PSA), skin or ovarian cancer; only breast, bowel, cervical and lung programs exist.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
There is no effective population screen for ovarian cancer, and CA 125 plus ultrasound is not a national program. One relative diagnosed at 72 does not by itself open a high-risk mutation pathway. The oral contraceptive pill is not a screening test.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. A single normal CA 125 today ends her familial risk: A marker does not close a family history, and it is not the screen.
C. CA 125 every 6 months can replace the ultrasound: A shorter marker interval is still not a program.
D. Enrol her in annual CA 125 and pelvic ultrasound: The clinic has invented a BreastScreen equivalent. That pair does not perform as a program.
E. Start a combined oral contraceptive as the screening test: Contraception is not surveillance.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
No national ovarian screening program exists.

items.question_text: A 49-year-old woman requests her first bowel cancer screening kit. She is asymptomatic, with no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit, and no weight loss. She believes she is already in the automatic mail-out group because she is nearly 50 and has heard that kits arrive from 50. At 49 she is not yet in the mailed cohort. There is no family history that would move her to colonoscopy instead. Examination is normal. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Colonoscopy is the first program test at 49
She should wait until she has a symptom before requesting a kit
She needs to request the first kit rather than wait for a mail-out
She cannot screen until 50, so a request now will be rejected
A kit will be mailed automatically within the year, so she should wait for it
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. She needs to request the first kit rather than wait for a mail-out

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
At 49 the first bowel kit is requested. It is not mailed automatically, and she does not wait until 50.

2. THE RULE
People aged 45-49 may request a free NBCSP iFOBT kit, automatic mail-out runs from 50 to 74, and recent colonoscopy surveillance replaces the kit.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
At 49 she is in the 45–49 band. The first kit is requested. Automatic mailing is what her neighbour received at 51. Once she completes a kit, later kits are mailed every 2 years. Symptoms would be a reason not to use the kit.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Colonoscopy is the first program test at 49: The program test is the immunochemical kit.
B. She should wait until she has a symptom before requesting a kit: A symptom would take her off screening and onto diagnostic assessment.
D. She cannot screen until 50, so a request now will be rejected: She can request a kit now. Fifty is the mail-out birthday, not the eligibility birthday.
E. A kit will be mailed automatically within the year, so she should wait for it: She has mapped her neighbour's path onto her own age.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
45–49 request. 50–74 are mailed.

---

items.question_text: A 46-year-old woman finds a firm lump in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast. It has been there for three weeks. She is otherwise well, has no family history of breast cancer, and has never had a mammogram. She asks to be enrolled in BreastScreen so the lump can be checked on the program. A receptionist has told her the next screening round is in six months and she should wait. BreastScreen is a screening program for women without symptoms. A new lump is a diagnostic problem, not a screening invitation. She needs clinical assessment and diagnostic imaging, not a place on a screening list. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Refer for diagnostic triple assessment rather than a screening mammogram
Enrol her in BreastScreen and wait for the next round
Arrange a screening mammogram only, with no clinical examination
Reassure her that a firm lump at 46 is benign and review in a year
Start tamoxifen while waiting for the screening appointment
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Refer for diagnostic triple assessment rather than a screening mammogram

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A 46-year-old woman finds a firm lump in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast. It has been there for three weeks. She is otherwise well, has no family history of breast cancer, and has never had a mammogram.

2. THE RULE
A breast symptom or high familial risk needs diagnostic or specialist assessment, not a routine BreastScreen mammogram.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
A woman with a breast symptom is not a screening candidate. BreastScreen is for asymptomatic women in the eligible age range. A new lump needs diagnostic assessment, not a screening invitation. Waiting for the next round, or arranging only a screening mammogram, delays proper assessment.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Enrol her in BreastScreen and wait for the next round: A palpable lump is a symptom; screening rounds are not for symptomatic women and delay diagnosis.
C. Arrange a screening mammogram only, with no clinical examination: Imaging alone omits clinical examination and biopsy; triple assessment needs all three.
D. Reassure her that a firm lump at 46 is benign and review in a year: Age 46 does not make a new firm lump benign; it needs assessment now, not in a year.
E. Start tamoxifen while waiting for the screening appointment: Tamoxifen is not a diagnostic step and has no role before a diagnosis.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
A breast symptom or high familial risk needs diagnostic or specialist assessment, not a routine BreastScreen mammogram.

---

items.question_text: A 55-year-old man with no personal or family history of melanoma asks to be enrolled in a national skin-cancer screening program. He has read that Australia has the highest rate of melanoma and assumes there must be a mail-out or invitation program like BreastScreen. He has no changing moles and no symptom. A colleague says to enrol him in the national melanoma screen and arrange annual full-body photography on the program. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Explain there is no national melanoma screening program to enrol him in
Enrol him in the national melanoma screening program and arrange annual photography
Start annual PSA screening because there is a national prostate program
Arrange a CA-125 and pelvic ultrasound as part of average-risk ovarian screening
Reassure him that melanoma does not occur in Australia
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Explain there is no national melanoma screening program to enrol him in

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A 55-year-old man with no personal or family history of melanoma asks to be enrolled in a national skin-cancer screening program. He has read that Australia has the highest rate of melanoma and assumes there must be a mail-out or invitation program like BreastScreen. He has no changing moles and no symptom.

2. THE RULE
Australia has no national population screening program for prostate (PSA), skin or ovarian cancer; only breast, bowel, cervical and lung programs exist.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Australia has no national population screening program for melanoma, average-risk ovarian cancer, or prostate cancer. A high incidence does not create a program. He should not be enrolled in a screen that does not exist. Sun protection and review of changing lesions is the advice, not a fictional program.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Enrol him in the national melanoma screening program and arrange annual photography: Australia has no national melanoma screening program to enrol him in.
C. Start annual PSA screening because there is a national prostate program: There is no national prostate screening program, and PSA is unrelated to melanoma.
D. Arrange a CA-125 and pelvic ultrasound as part of average-risk ovarian screening: Ovarian screening with CA-125 and ultrasound is not recommended and is irrelevant to his question.
E. Reassure him that melanoma does not occur in Australia: Australia has one of the highest melanoma rates in the world; this is false.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Australia has no national population screening program for prostate (PSA), skin or ovarian cancer; only breast, bowel, cervical and lung programs exist.

---
